title: Code Review Anti-Patterns
summary: Review cultures fail in recognizable ways — rubber-stamping, nitpick floods, drive-by blocks, gatekeeping, and one senior as the bottleneck. Each has a specific cause and a specific counter-move.

slides.markdown:
Broken review cultures don't look broken from inside. Every PR gets approved, the dashboard is green, and nobody says "our review process is theater" out loud.

The failure modes are recognizable, though, and each has a distinct cause: rubber-stamping comes from overload, nitpick floods come from a reviewer with no framework for prioritizing, drive-by blocks come from missing follow-up norms, and gatekeeping comes from unwritten design authority.

The useful thing about naming them is that each has a **specific counter-move** — usually a process change, not a conversation about being nicer. This topic goes through the seven that show up most, what causes each, and what to actually do.

slides.subTitle: "LGTM" in ninety seconds
slides.markdown:
The approval that arrives four minutes after a 900-line PR opened. Nobody read it, and everyone knows it.

Blaming the reviewer misses the cause, which is almost always **structural**:

- The PR is too big to evaluate, so approving is the only exit (see [review process and tooling](review-process-and-tooling)).
- Two approvers are required, so each assumes the other read it closely.
- Review is unrewarded work squeezed between the reviewer's own deadlines.
- The author is senior, and disagreeing costs more socially than it appears to be worth.

What catches it: **change failure rate against review throughput**. If review is fast and thorough on paper while defects keep reaching production, review isn't catching what you think it is.

The counters are mechanical — cap PR size, drop from two required approvers to one accountable one, and make review time explicitly part of the sprint rather than an unfunded tax. Telling people to "review more carefully" changes nothing, because nobody chose to be careless.

slides.subTitle: One real bug, twenty trivia
slides.markdown:
Twenty-three comments on a PR: nineteen about naming and comment wording, three about test style, and one — number fourteen — pointing out that the retry loop will double-charge a customer.

The author, drowning, mechanically applies all twenty-three. The double-charge gets "fixed" with the least-thought change that makes the comment go away. **Signal buried in volume is the same as no signal.**

The counter is prioritization the reviewer does *for* the author, not effort the author has to spend sorting:

- **Label every comment.** `blocking:` / `suggestion:` / `nit:`. Conventional Comments formalizes this, and reviewdog can enforce the prefix in CI.
- **Lead the review** with a summary comment: "One blocking issue — the retry path on line 88. The rest are nits, take or leave them."
- **Cap yourself.** Past roughly five nits, stop writing them and ask whether the formatter or linter should own that category instead.

Worth checking your own reviews for: if your last ten had a 10:1 nit-to-substance ratio, you're generating cost, not catching bugs.

slides.subTitle: Request changes, then vanish
slides.markdown:
A reviewer clicks **Request changes** with one comment, then goes on vacation, or onto a different project, or simply never opens the tab again. The PR is now hard-blocked by someone who isn't coming back, and platform defaults require *that person* to clear it.

This is more corrosive than a slow review, because the author can't even escalate cleanly — the blocker isn't refusing, they're absent, and there's nobody to argue with.

The fixes are policy, not politeness:

- **A stale-block rule.** "A change request that gets no response within 24 hours of the author replying can be resolved by another owner." Write it down so using it isn't a social act.
- **Blocking implies a commitment to re-review**, same as any other review SLA. If you can't come back, leave the comment without blocking and say "non-blocking, worth a look."
- **Escalate to the team, not the person.** "PR #421 is blocked on a comment from Sam, who's out until the 12th — can another owner take a look?"

The author's move in the meantime: address the comment, reply explaining what you changed, and tag a second owner. Never sit on it waiting.

slides.subTitle: Relitigating a settled decision
slides.markdown:
The design was agreed in a doc three weeks ago. The implementation PR arrives and a reviewer who wasn't in that discussion comments: "why are we using an event queue here at all? A synchronous call would be simpler."

The question isn't unreasonable — asked three weeks earlier it was exactly the right question. Asked now, at implementation time, it costs a week and puts the author in the position of defending a decision they didn't unilaterally make.

What separates gatekeeping from legitimate concern is **new information**. If the reviewer has learned something the design discussion didn't have — a constraint, a benchmark, an incident — reopening is correct. If it's a preference that simply wasn't voiced in time, it belongs in a follow-up, not as a block on this PR.

The script that resolves it without a fight:

> "That was decided in the design doc — here's the thread. If the trade-off looks wrong now, let's reopen it there rather than in this PR, and I'll keep this one scoped to the agreed design."

That redirects to the right forum instead of arguing the merits, which is why it works even when the reviewer outranks you.

One engineer is on every PR — sometimes by `CODEOWNERS`, more often by habit, because they wrote most of the service and reviews feel safer with them on it.

The costs compound in both directions. Their queue sets the team's delivery speed and they get no uninterrupted time to build anything. Meanwhile nobody else's review skill develops, because they never have to be the one who catches something, and the knowledge concentration that caused this gets *worse* every sprint.

Breaking it deliberately:

- **Pair review for a few weeks.** The senior and a second reviewer both read, then compare notes. That's how review judgement transfers — reading alongside someone, not reading a checklist.
- **Narrow `CODEOWNERS` to the genuinely dangerous paths.** Payments and migrations, not `*`.
- **Let the senior review the review.** For a while they read after someone else has approved, commenting only on what was missed. Two rounds of that and the second reviewer's catch rate visibly moves.

The honest blocker is usually that the senior finds it faster to review everything themselves. That's true this sprint and false by the third one.

slides.subTitle: Rewriting the PR in the thread
slides.markdown:
A reviewer opens a PR that solves the problem in a way they wouldn't have chosen, and proceeds to reconstruct their own version across eighteen inline comments — a different abstraction here, a different data structure there, a suggestion to split this class.

Each comment may be defensible. Together they're a demand to rewrite a working change to match one person's taste, delivered in the most expensive possible format: thirty comment round-trips at hours apart each.

Two signals that you've crossed into it: the diff after your comments would be unrecognizable to its author, and none of your comments name a **defect** — only a preference.

What to do instead when a PR is genuinely built wrong:

- **Say it once, at the top, as one comment.** "I think this belongs in the domain layer rather than the controller — that's a big change, so let's talk before you rewrite anything." One conversation, not eighteen.
- **Then take it off the PR.** A fifteen-minute call decides a structural disagreement that a comment thread will spend two days on.
- **Ask whether it's worth it now.** A working, tested change that's structurally imperfect may be worth merging with a follow-up ticket — especially if it's behind a flag.

slides.subTitle: Not all slow review is bad review
slides.markdown:
Review is supposed to create some friction. The question is whether the friction is buying anything:

| | Healthy friction | Unhealthy friction |
|---|---|---|
| **What's raised** | a defect, a missing edge case, a security hole | a preference, a style choice, a settled decision |
| **Cost to author** | one focused round trip | many rounds, unclear what's required |
| **Who can resolve it** | the author, from the comment alone | only the reviewer, and only in their own time |
| **Effect on the next PR** | author internalizes the pattern | author writes smaller, more defensive changes to avoid review |
| **Symptom** | fewer defects reach prod | delivery slows with no change in defect rate |

The diagnostic that cuts through the argument is the bottom row. **Slow review plus a falling change failure rate is working.** Slow review plus an unchanged one is pure tax — the friction is real and it's buying nothing.

That's why measuring both matters. Teams that track only cycle time optimize toward rubber-stamping; teams that track only thoroughness optimize toward gatekeeping.

slides.subTitle: One issue revealed per round
slides.markdown:
Round one: "rename this method." Author pushes a fix. Round two: "now that I look closer, the error handling is wrong." Round three: "also this needs a test." Round four: "actually, should this be async?"

Six days for a change that had four issues, all of which were visible on day one. Each round costs a full turnaround plus the author reloading context, so the total is far worse than the sum of the reviews.

The reviewer-side fix is **one complete pass before commenting**. Read the whole diff, then write everything you found, then hit submit — GitHub's "start a review" batches comments precisely so you don't send them one at a time.

Special case worth naming: if you spot a fundamental problem in the first two minutes, say *only* that and stop. "Before I review in detail — this looks like it duplicates the existing `RetryPolicy`; is that intentional?" Reviewing the details of code that's about to be deleted wastes both people's time.

And once a PR has been through a couple of rounds, hold yourself to what's already been raised. New nits discovered on round three are usually the reviewer getting bored, not the code getting worse.

slides.sectionTitle: When the team stops believing in review
slides.subTitle: The end state
slides.markdown:
The terminal condition: everyone still opens PRs, everyone still approves them, and nobody believes review catches anything. It's now a merge formality with extra latency.

How you can tell it's happened:

- Median time-to-approve is minutes on changes of any size.
- Comments are almost entirely nits, because substance stopped being raised.
- Post-incident reviews routinely find the bug was visible in a diff that two people approved.
- Authors are surprised — mildly annoyed, even — when someone actually asks a question.

The reason this is hard to recover from is that the metrics look **excellent**. Fast cycle time, 100% review coverage, high approval rate. Nothing in a dashboard says "review coverage: complete, review value: zero."

Recovery starts with evidence, not exhortation. Take the last three incidents, find whether the cause was reviewable in the diff, and show the team. "Two of our last three outages were visible in a PR that got an LGTM in under five minutes" restarts the conversation in a way that a reminder about review standards never does.

Then change one structural thing — PR size caps, or a single accountable approver — and re-measure. Culture follows the constraint.

slides.sectionTitle: Changing a review culture you don't manage
slides.markdown:
You're an IC. The review culture is bad. You have no authority to change policy. This comes up constantly and there is more leverage here than people assume.

What actually moves it:

- **Model it in your own reviews first.** Label comments `blocking:` / `nit:`, lead with a summary of what matters, and reply to your own PRs with the reasoning behind pushback. Prefix conventions spread by imitation faster than by decree — two people doing it is usually enough to seed a team.
- **Ship a tool change instead of a policy change.** Adding `black` and a pre-commit hook needs one PR and no meeting, and it deletes the entire style-comment category permanently.
- **Make the cost visible with data, not complaints.** "Our p90 PR is 850 lines and median time-to-first-comment is 2.1 days" is a conversation; "reviews here are slow" is a mood.
- **Use retros for the pattern, 1:1s for the person.** A specific reviewer nitpicking is a private conversation. Everyone nitpicking is a team norm to raise in retro.

One caution: pick one thing at a time. A teammate who arrives with a six-point review-process manifesto gets ignored regardless of how right they are.

Every anti-pattern here has the same shape: **a structural problem that presents as a personality problem.**

Rubber-stamping looks like laziness and is usually PR size plus unfunded review time. Nitpick overload looks like pedantry and is usually a missing labeling convention and an absent formatter. The drive-by block looks like rudeness and is a missing stale-block policy. Gatekeeping looks like ego and is usually undocumented design authority.

That's why the counter-move is nearly always a constraint rather than a conversation. "Please review more carefully" has never fixed a review culture; a 400-line cap and one accountable approver routinely has.

The exception worth naming: genuinely hostile review — comments about the person rather than the code — is not a process problem and doesn't have a process fix. That's a direct conversation, and if it doesn't change, a manager one.

Next in this group: real-time collaboration as an alternative to async review — [pair and mob programming](pair-and-mob-programming) — where several of these failure modes simply don't have room to form.
